KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) is virtualization infrastructure native to the Linux kernel, turning the Linux operating system itself into a Type-1 hypervisor. Since merging into the Linux 2.6.20 mainline kernel in 2007, KVM has become a cornerstone of global cloud infrastructure. Major platforms including Google Cloud, AWS Nitro, OpenStack, and Proxmox VE are built on KVM.

The core idea of virtualization is to run multiple isolated operating system instances on a single physical machine. An intermediate software layer manages physical resources (CPU, memory, disk, and network), abstracts them into virtual resources, and allocates them to individual virtual machines (guest VMs).
The hypervisor sits between hardware and guests; actual performance varies with implementation and workload
The hypervisor runs as a process on the host OS, introducing additional overhead
1.2 Where KVM fits in the classification
KVM’s classification is the subject of a familiar "philosophical debate":

Position A (KVM is Type-1): KVM is a kernel module (kvm.ko). Once loaded, the Linux kernel itself becomes a hypervisor, directly controlling hardware virtualization capabilities (VT-x/AMD-V). Guest VMs run as separate processes. The hypervisor component operates in Ring 0.
Position B (KVM is Type-2): KVM still runs on a full Linux OS, relying on the host OS scheduler, memory management, drivers, and other facilities. KVM cannot operate without the Linux kernel.

The mainstream consensus Academia and industry generally classify KVM as a Type-1 (Bare Metal) hypervisor. The central argument is that KVM integrates the hypervisor’s core functions (CPU and memory virtualization) into kernel space (Ring 0). Guest VMs execute directly in VMX non-root mode without passing through host user space. Here, Linux serves not as a "Host OS" but as a general foundation providing low-level services: scheduling, memory management, and the I/O driver stack.

CPU flags only establish that the current environment exposes the corresponding capabilities. Firmware enablement, nested virtualization restrictions, kernel modules, /dev/kvm permissions, and the actual result of starting QEMU must be checked separately. BIOS/UEFI settings Many motherboards disable virtualization extensions by default. Before using KVM, enable Intel VT-x or AMD SVM in BIOS/UEFI. Enterprise servers such as Dell PowerEdge and HPE ProLiant typically enable them by default.
KVM became the de facto standard for Linux virtualization primarily because of its "the kernel is the hypervisor" design:
CPU execution can use hardware virtualization; VM exits, device emulation, and ioctl still incur overhead, so performance varies with workload
Schedulers (CFS/EEVDF), memory management (THP, KSM), cgroups resource limits, NUMA awareness, filesystems, and the network stack
SELinux (sVirt), AppArmor, and seccomp apply directly to QEMU processes to provide VM-level security isolation
All hardware drivers supported by Linux are automatically available to the host; no separate driver stack needs maintenance
KVM code is part of the mainline Linux kernel and evolves with kernel releases, avoiding vendor lock-in
GPLv2-licensed, with no commercial licensing fees
2. KVM + QEMU: cooperation between kernel and user space

KVM itself is responsible only for CPU and memory virtualization, the performance-critical path that must run in kernel space. Emulating peripherals such as disks, network cards, graphics cards, and USB devices requires a user-space program. In the Linux ecosystem, QEMU fills that role.
Device emulation (disk/network/GPU/USB), VM lifecycle management, and guest memory allocation
CPU virtualization (VMX/SVM), memory virtualization (EPT/NPT), and virtual device interrupt injection
Provides VMX root/non-root modes and hardware-accelerated page-table walks

KVM exposes its user-space interface through the /dev/kvm character device. The control interface between QEMU and KVM primarily uses file descriptors and ioctl(), with mmap sharing runtime state. Modern I/O paths may also involve ioeventfd, irqfd, and vhost.
Intel VT-x introduces two CPU modes:
VMX Root Mode: the mode in which the hypervisor (KVM) runs. It can execute VMLAUNCH/VMRESUME instructions to enter the guest.
VMX Non-Root Mode: the mode in which guest VMs run. On a sensitive instruction or event, the CPU automatically triggers a VM Exit back to root mode.

The VMCS (Virtual Machine Control Structure) is the central data structure of this mechanism, maintained by KVM in kernel space. It stores the complete context of host and guest state (control registers, segment registers, MSRs, and so on). QEMU in user space cannot access the VMCS directly.
There are two approaches to memory virtualization:
KVM maintains a shadow translation table from guest VA -> host PA and intercepts guest page-table changes
CPU hardware directly supports two-stage page-table walks: GVA -> GPA (guest page tables) -> HPA (EPT/NPT page tables)
Near bare-metal performance, with fewer VM exits

EPT/NPT is key to KVM’s near-native performance. It eliminates VM exits triggered by guest page-table modifications: the guest can change its own page tables as a native system would, while hardware performs two-stage address translation transparently in the background.

The value of QEMU’s pure emulation
QEMU’s TCG can emulate systems across instruction sets, such as emulating ARM on an x86 host. It does not use same-architecture KVM acceleration, and performance differences must be measured against actual workloads. This kind of system emulation is useful for embedded development, reverse engineering, and firmware testing.

On an x86 host, choose the module that matches the CPU; do not run both Intel and AMD examples on the same machine. Whether nested=1 is necessary depends on the kernel defaults. ignore_msrs=1 is a compatibility-debugging option that can hide MSR issues, not a general-purpose tuning default.
3. libvirt: a unified management abstraction layer
Managing VMs directly with the QEMU command line becomes seriously problematic as the deployment grows:
libvirt’s goal is to provide a unified management interface for different hypervisors. Its core benefits are:
All VM parameters are defined in one XML file that can be version-controlled, audited, and migrated
The same virsh command manages KVM, Xen, LXC, and VMware, making the hypervisor type transparent to higher layers
virtqemud manages the VM lifecycle, including automatic startup, shutdown, and restart
Unified management of virtual networks (NAT/bridged) and storage pools (LVM/ZFS/Ceph/directories)
Deep SELinux/sVirt integration, with a separate security label for each VM

Traditional libvirt uses a single libvirtd daemon for all functionality. libvirt supports both monolithic and modular daemon deployments. Whether a distribution uses the modular design depends on its packages and service configuration, not simply its libvirt version. In a modular deployment, each driver runs in a separate process:

Security isolation: each daemon has a separate attack surface. This narrows the scope of shared processes, but shared privileges, host resources, and networks can still allow effects to cross boundaries; it does not guarantee that VMs remain unaffected.
Independent restarts: QEMU processes are independent, so restarting a management daemon usually does not shut down guests. Management operations, connections, and ongoing jobs may still be affected.
Install only what is needed: a containerized environment can install just libvirt-daemon-driver-qemu without the full dependency set.
Socket activation: systemd manages sockets and starts daemons on demand, reducing idle-service overhead.
Compatibility transition Many distributions still offer libvirtd as a compatibility option. Check which mode your system uses:
libvirt uses a URI to specify the target hypervisor to connect to:
System-level management connection; the distribution and qemu.conf determine which identity QEMU runs under
User privileges; VMs run as ordinary user processes
SSH tunnel; works out of the box without additional certificates
Mutual TLS authentication, suitable for environments with multiple administrators

virt-manager is a GTK-based desktop application that manages KVM/Xen/LXC VMs through the libvirt protocol. It suits workstations and personal use, and is also useful for "emergency manual operations" on production servers.
VM creation wizard: graphically configure CPU, memory, disks, and networking to generate libvirt XML
Hardware hotplug: add or remove virtual disks and network cards while running (requires guest support)
SPICE/VNC console: built-in remote desktop connections with clipboard sharing and USB redirection
Snapshot management: create, restore, and delete VM snapshots (internal snapshots use qcow2; support depends on disk format, firmware, TPM, and current software versions; a snapshot is not a backup)
Performance monitoring: real-time graphs of CPU usage, memory use, and disk/network I/O
Lightweight SPICE/VNC client for connecting to VM consoles without launching the full virt-manager
Command-line VM creation tool suitable for scripted or automated deployments
Clones an existing VM, automatically handling conflicts such as MAC addresses and disk images
Resets or cleans VM images for template-based deployment by removing SSH host keys, machine IDs, logs, and similar state
Quickly builds VM images using a process similar to a Dockerfile build
Red Hat’s web management interface, with VM management provided through a Cockpit plugin

KVM’s host kernel is Linux; guest OS support in the table does not mean KVM can run as a Windows host kernel module. Containers share the host kernel, and migration mechanisms such as CRIU also have compatibility constraints.
This is the most common technology-selection question. The two are complementary rather than substitutes.

A common combination: KVM + containers
A common deployment uses VMs to provide different kernels and tenant boundaries, with applications running in containers inside the VMs. This does not mean that every public cloud uses KVM. Different platforms use different hypervisors; Azure’s virtualization foundation, for example, should not be classified as KVM.
KVM is the dominant choice for Linux cloud infrastructure:
Google was one of KVM’s early major contributors
AWS builds on KVM with its own Nitro cards to offload I/O
OpenStack Nova uses the libvirt/KVM driver by default
Open-source virtualization management platform, using KVM for VMs and LXC for containers
Red Hat’s enterprise virtualization solution, positioned against VMware vSphere
Supports several hypervisors, with KVM the most commonly used
Summary KVM is not "a single piece of software" but a virtualization stack of cooperating layers:
KVM kernel module: provides hardware acceleration for CPU and memory
QEMU: provides device emulation and platform modeling
libvirt: provides a unified management API and toolchain
libguestfs/virt- tools*: provide image manipulation and automation
Understanding the responsibility boundaries of these four layers is the key to mastering the KVM virtualization stack.
